FIX AS IMPLEMENTED (PR 2.6b): both lanes restore via .github/actions/restore-aria-state (state checkout, then the binding migration, then the store environment exported to GITHUB_ENV) and publish via `state publish` under an FF-only push; the artifact is demoted to a run-scoped forensic copy no code path restores from; the workflow contract registry moves with the YAML (contents:write, github_git, one store-rooted write path, run-scoped artifact name pinned so a future fixed name fails the contract). TWO DEFECTS THE YAML-ONLY CUTOVER WOULD HAVE SHIPPED, both found by reading the round trip rather than the diff: (1) a restored store is not yet a usable tools root - the branch deliberately does not carry repo_identity.json because it records a runner-absolute bound_repo_root - and only aria-auto-cycle ran the binding migration, so the executor's first restored run would have died at its lease check on ambiguous_tools_root; the migration moved into the shared action. (2) seed_drift_findings.py wrote to <checkout>/aria-findings while the kernel reads through repo_state_root, which the restore binds at the store, so every night would have seeded a full pool where nothing looks; it imports the kernel's resolver now. VALIDATION LIMIT to state plainly: both lanes run on [self-hosted, linux, claude] and no runner is currently attached, so this lands reviewed, contract-verified and locally tested but UNEXERCISED; the first real nightly is the proof. Do NOT mark Wave 1 complete until that run exists. OPERATOR PRECONDITION: the aria/state branch ruleset (block force-push + deletions) must exist BEFORE any bootstrap, then vars.ARIA_STATE_BOOTSTRAP_ACK - see docs/runbooks/aria-state-branch-bootstrap.md.

title: The state_continuity gate freezes the first cycle after the lane cutover: its probe walks only the tools root while the published reference covers all three, so healthy workspace and repo surfaces read as lost, and a freshly built probe can never satisfy the chain-linkage test it is judged by
rule_violated: `_phase_state_continuity` built its probe snapshot with `roots={"tools": base_dir}` and compared it against `resolve_continuity_reference`, which after the lane cutover returns the PUBLISHED SNAPSHOT — a manifest covering tools + workspace + repo. `snapshot_continuity` computes lost_surfaces as reference-minus-current, so every workspace-root and repo-root surface the store publishes (16 declared) is reported LOST on a completely healthy tree. Independently, the probe is built fresh with no `previous`, so its `prev_manifest_root` is None and `snapshots_are_linked` returns False for every tree that has ever existed, giving `chain_broken`. Either fault alone yields GAP_CRITICAL, and `ContinuityVerdict.blocks_action` is True for critical, so `freeze_autonomous_writes` trips the `state_integrity_gap` breaker and every subsequent cycle is refused at `_cycle_preflight`. Reproduced against real git before the fix: STATUS=critical, reasons=('state_continuity_chain_broken:...got_prev=None', 'state_continuity_surfaces_lost:repo_finding_index').
notes: WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE UNTIL NOW, which is the pattern rather than the excuse: `resolve_continuity_reference` returned None on every lane, because no store was checked out and the committed daily anchors all predate the `state_manifest_root` field. With no reference the verdict is `unknown`, which blocks nothing - recorded in PROGRESS.md as 'the gate reports unknown every night'. The cutover (249a5e940) created the reference, and both faults went live in the same instant. A gate that has never had a reference proves nothing about a gate that has one; this is the third instance this programme has found of a control that was correct until its input existed. FIX: (1) `continuity_probe_roots` derives the probe's roots from `store_roots` when a store is bound, falling back to tools-only when it is not - imported rather than restated, because a second copy of the three-root mapping is how two roots come out right and the third silently wrong; (2) descent is measured where it is actually decided - `store_is_at_published_tip` compares the store worktree's HEAD against the remote tip, since `publish_state` pushes fast-forward-only and `checkout_state_store` establishes the tree AT the tip. Passing the reference in as `previous` to make the linkage test pass was REJECTED: that would assert the very thing under examination. The transport proof replaces the linkage half ONLY; the lost-surface half is untouched, because loss is the question no transport can answer and the one the gate exists for. Refusals now name both SHAs (head=X tip=Y) rather than 'chain broken', which is a fetch away from fixed. Mutation-checked three ways: ignoring the proof, a proof that can only say yes, and reverting the probe roots each fail the suite. VALIDATION LIMIT: as with the cutover itself, this is verified locally against real git repositories and remains UNEXERCISED on the self-hosted runner.

title: The first restored night can run a full cycle and then be refused permission to persist it: a restored workspace has ledgers but no identity file, which ensure_workspace refuses outright and integrity verify reports as workspace_migration_required, and both lanes gate publication on that verdict
rule_violated: The workspace identity file is host-local (it records this runner's absolute repo_root) and correctly does not travel on the shared `aria/state` branch; the workspace LEDGERS do travel. So the ordinary shape of a restored workspace is rows-present, identity-absent. `ensure_workspace` (workspace.py:311-313) raised RuntimeError('workspace_migration_required') for exactly that shape, and `_verify_workspace` (integrity.py:122) bootstrapped only when the identity was absent AND every ledger was empty - so a restored workspace skipped the bootstrap, `workspace_contract_version` read a file that was not there, returned 0, and the verdict became `workspace_migration_required`. Both lanes gate publication on `steps.integrity.outputs.state_valid == 'true'` (aria-auto-cycle.yml, aria-agent-executor.yml), so a restored store does its night's work and is then refused permission to persist it. This is the identical shape to the tools root's `ambiguous_tools_root`, which got a governed migration (`migrate_tools_bootstrap`, wired into the restore action); the workspace sibling got no repair path at all.
notes: LATENT UNTIL TONIGHT. The first live nightly (2026-08-04) was a BOOTSTRAP - it created the workspace identity locally, so neither branch fired. Tonight is the first RESTORE, which is when both do. MEASURED against a store restored from a published tip carrying real workspace ledger content: `integrity status: drift` before the fix, `ok` after, with the ledger rows intact. FIX: re-derive the identity instead of refusing. Safe because the workspace PATH already carries the binding - `workspace_paths` keys the directory by repository hash, so a workspace at <base>/<hash> cannot belong to another repository - and the identity-mismatch branch above still refuses a disagreeing identity. What the blanket refusal actually protected against, content this kernel cannot read, is caught downstream and more precisely by `_verify_workspace`'s per-ledger `verify_jsonl`, which names the offending ledger. The re-derivation is recorded as `workspace_identity_rederived` so it is auditable rather than silent. Found by a workflow sweep for controls that were correct only while `aria/state` had no published reference; it confirmed seventeen, and this is the one that breaks tonight.

title: store_is_at_published_tip maps an unreadable remote to a positive finding of amnesia, so one transient git ls-remote failure freezes the nightly on a healthy tree
rule_violated: `_remote_tip` returns None for ANY non-zero `git ls-remote`, so it cannot distinguish 'the remote names a different commit' from 'the remote could not be reached'. `store_is_at_published_tip` collapsed both into `proven=False`, which `assess_memory_continuity` substitutes for the chain-linkage half, producing `chain_broken` -> GAP_CRITICAL -> `blocks_action` -> `freeze_autonomous_writes` -> `record_failure(kind='state_integrity_gap')` and an aborted cycle. The nightly runs 50-150 minutes and its ls-remote is unauthenticated (`persist-credentials: false`), so a single network blip or rate-limit reports memory loss that did not occur and stops the run. The code already knew the tip might be unreadable - it printed `tip=<unreadable>` in the refusal - and mapped it to amnesia anyway, contradicting this module's own doctrine that `unknown` is the honest answer when evidence is unavailable.
notes: MY OWN REGRESSION, introduced by 9d8b7929 (the fix for ORPHAN-CRITICAL-549) and caught by the sweep the same day. The doctrine it broke is quoted three lines above the code that broke it, which is the useful part of the lesson: restating a rule in a docstring is not the same as encoding it. FIX: `DescentProof` carries `readable`. An unreadable remote yields `unknown` (blocks nothing); a genuinely divergent store still yields `critical`; and real surface loss stays `critical` even when the remote cannot be read, because the tree is present and loss is evidence about it. All four cases measured: healthy+readable -> ok; healthy+unreadable -> unknown with blocks_action False; genuinely behind -> critical; unreadable + real loss -> critical.

title: The ledger appender and the tools migration disagree about the row format, so every restore re-chains the previous night's rows: the published tail_ledger_hash never survives one night, which makes contention replay structurally unable to replay
rule_violated: `append_declared_jsonl` writes ledger rows WITHOUT a `schema_version` field; `migrate_tools_v1_to_v2` / `v2_to_v3` stamp it and re-chain every row from the first unstamped one onward. The migration runs on EVERY restore, because `tools_contract_version` reads `repo_identity.json` and that file deliberately never travels on the state branch (it records a runner-absolute `bound_repo_root`). So each night the bind rewrites the rows the previous night appended, changing their `ledger_hash` and therefore the surface's `tail_ledger_hash`. Measured over the exact production loop (restore -> bind -> append -> publish -> restore -> bind), seeded with the REAL rows from the live aria/state branch: night 1 tail 9ec3d7f5 survives the bind (those rows already carry schema_version 3); the row appended that night carries schema_version=<ABSENT>; night 2 published tail 0127a841 becomes a7f8ed2b after the bind - SURVIVES=False. CONSEQUENCE: `append_only_suffix` proves the local prefix by comparing the row at the base's last index against the base's recorded tail hash. That comparison can never hold across a restore, so `publish_with_contention_replay` raises `replay_prefix_diverged` for every real contention between the 01:00 producer and the 02:00 executor - a lost publish race is unrecoverable rather than replayed. The same refusal blocks `memory_gap.restore_and_replay`.
notes: NOT AN EMERGENCY FOR TONIGHT, and the distinction matters. The nightly is single-lane, so nothing contends; and `state_continuity` now proves descent by comparing the store worktree's HEAD against the remote tip (commit SHAs), not by row hashes, so the gate is unaffected. The defect bites when the 02:00 executor genuinely races the 01:00 producer, and when recovery is needed. FOUND BY RUNNING, AND MY FIRST TWO READINGS WERE BOTH WRONG: reading the migration suggested 'no re-chain after the first night' (a two-night test agreed, because row 0 stabilises while the TAIL keeps moving), and a sandbox test suggested 'every night from the start' (wrong for the live tree, whose rows already carry schema_version 3). Only the exact production loop, seeded with the real branch rows, gave the true shape. ROOT CAUSE: two writers, one file, two formats - the migration keeps 'fixing' what the appender wrote. FIX SHAPE: make `append_declared_jsonl` write the current contract's `schema_version` itself, so the migration is content-idempotent and the chain is stable across restores (tier 1 - the unstamped row cannot exist). A second, complementary fix is to let the tree carry its own FORMAT version separately from the machine-local host binding, so the migration does not run on every restore at all; today `repo_identity.json` conflates a property of the TREE (contract version, must travel) with a property of the HOST (bound_repo_root, must not).

title: Every contention or recovery replay that carries a glob-fanned ledger refuses: the replay stages each suffix at a filename built from the snapshot's surface KEY, which for glob surfaces is name:relative/path, and re-appends with expected_surface set to that key, which the declared-surface gate rejects
rule_violated: Snapshot surface keys for glob surfaces are `name:relative/path` (the covered_tool_ledgers vocabulary, mirrored by _surface_entries). `rebase_store_onto_remote` staged each loser suffix at `staging / f"{key}.jsonl"` - a PATH into a nonexistent directory once the key carries `/` - and `replay_append_only_suffixes` asserted `expected_surface=<key>`, which `_assert_declared_surface` refuses because it speaks manifest names. The live aria/state tree carries glob-fanned ledgers (runs/by-cycle/*, agent-invocations/*, plans/*), so every real contention between the 01:00 producer and 02:00 executor, and every restore_and_replay recovery, would have refused - while the plain-surface unit tests all passed. Found by running the recovery against the real branch rows, not by reading it: the third instance this week of a control that was correct only while its real input did not exist.
notes: Fixed on claude/aria-state-recovery in the same commit that closes ORPHAN-HIGH-552: surface_key_name() added to state_manifest (the vocabulary owner), replay stages by ordinal, appends by manifest name. Pinned by test_a_glob_surface_survives_the_replay.

title: The restore bind is spelled as a migration, and the migration's rewrite permit expires 2026-12-31: on 2027-01-01 every nightly restore starts refusing, and until then each bind writes a full tools-tree backup plus ~9 migration-ceremony governance rows per night on a tree that needs only a binding
rule_violated: A restored aria/state tree needs a BINDING (mint repo_identity.json for this host), but the restore action reaches it through migrate_tools_bootstrap -> migrate_tools_v1_to_v2, which is a MIGRATION: it snapshots the whole tools tree into .backups/migration-v0-to-v2-<ts>, rewrites every covered ledger under _rewrite_migration_jsonl's legacy allowance (MIGRATION_REWRITE_EXPIRES_AT = 2026-12-31; _raw_jsonl_legacy_allowed requires expires_at > now, measured), and appends migration_started/copied/validated/finalized ceremony rows to governance.jsonl - measured at 9 rows per bind on the live tree. Three symptoms, one cause: binding and migrating are different operations sharing one code path. On 2027-01-01 the allowance lapses and every nightly restore dies at the bind step.
notes: Root fix is a bind-only operation for restored trees (tree carries its contract version; identity minting without ledger rewrite). Not attempted in the 552 commit deliberately: 552 makes the rewrite byte-idempotent so the bind is CORRECT today, and the bind-only redesign changes the restore action contract - separate change, separate proof.

title: run-protected-ssh.sh abandons the host-key scan on any advertised key ssh-keygen cannot parse, exiting mutely with the pinned key still unexamined; the same pipeline can be killed by SIGPIPE
rule_violated: The candidate host-key loop parsed each advertised key with `printf '%s\n' "${candidate_key}" | ssh-keygen -lf - -E sha256 | awk ...` under `set -euo pipefail`. Two consequences, both measured. (1) SEMANTICS: `ssh-keygen -lf -` exits non-zero on a line it cannot parse, and `set -e` then ends the whole script mid-loop - so a host advertising an algorithm this ssh-keygen build cannot read aborts the backup at exit 255, before the loop reaches the PINNED key sitting on the next line. The abort carries no `die` reason, in a script where every other failure path names itself, and the correct refusal ('did not match exactly one advertised host key') sits three lines below the loop it never reaches. The foreseeable trigger is an OpenSSH upgrade on the droplet advertising a newer algorithm than the runner's ssh-keygen implements, which stops the nightly backup with an unexplained status. (2) STATUS FRAGILITY: `ssh-keygen -lf -` need not drain stdin, so under `pipefail` the writer can be signalled SIGPIPE - deterministically exit 141 once an advertised line exceeds the pipe buffer, and a scheduling race below it, which is how this production-secret invariant became a flaky red on an unrelated PR (#1085, run 31033608889).
notes: Registered with add-explicit at 559 rather than the next free number: 557 and 558 are allocated to a parallel session's in-flight renumber, and taking them would collide in the chain.

title: markdownlint-changed.mjs reports a missing linter as a lint failure: spawn ENOENT collapses to a bare exit 1 with no rule named, so 'the docs are bad' and 'nothing was checked' are indistinguishable
rule_violated: `process.exitCode = result.status ?? 1` treats spawnSync's launch failure (status null, `error` set with code ENOENT) as a lint failure. CI installs markdownlint-cli globally so the gate works there; a developer or agent checkout without it gets exit 1 and ZERO output, which reads as 'your documents failed lint' when the truth is 'no document was checked'. Measured three times in one session: a clean tree reported a red doc gate, and the only way to learn otherwise was to re-run the linter by hand via npx. A gate whose failure names no reason trains its readers to discount it - the same defect class as ORPHAN-HIGH-559 in the same session, in the tool that gates that finding's own review document.
notes: Registered with add-explicit at 560 to stay clear of 557/558, allocated to a parallel session's in-flight renumber.

title: One torn write permanently bricks a governed ledger: an unparseable trailing line - the ordinary residue of a crash mid-append - makes every subsequent READ and WRITE of that surface raise LedgerIntegrityError, so a single interrupted process ends the mission layer until a human repairs the file by hand
rule_violated: `_append_jsonl_locked_body` writes a row with one `os.write` + `os.fsync`; a crash between them can leave a partial final line, which is the ORDINARY residue of an interrupted append and not evidence of tampering. `_verify_jsonl_from_text` wraps the whole line walk in one try/except, so a `json.JSONDecodeError` anywhere - including on the LAST line - returns valid=False, and both `load_jsonl(verify=True)` and `_verify_existing_declared_chain_before_append` then raise. Measured on a mission ledger seeded with two good rows plus a truncated third: `fold_mission` RAISED LedgerIntegrityError and `transition_mission` REFUSED - so the surface can be neither read nor advanced. Every strict-read declared surface shares this path, so the blast radius is the whole state manifest, not missions alone. The two conditions are distinguishable and must not share a verdict: an unparseable LAST line with a hash-verified prefix is a torn write, and the incomplete row was never acknowledged to any caller (the append returns only after fsync), so discarding it loses nothing; an unparseable line in the MIDDLE, or any ledger_hash mismatch on a complete row, is corruption or tampering and must stay fatal. This directly contradicts PLAN Wave 2's completion criterion - 'crash-injection testlerinin tamamında mission kaldigi yerden devam eder' - under which a crash mid-write means NO mission continues.
notes: Found while building the Wave 2 crash-injection suite, by asking what residue a crash actually leaves rather than by racing a SIGKILL. Deliberately NOT fixed in the discovering commit: ledger.py is the kernel's most load-bearing module and the change landed hours before a nightly whose executor lane was already failing.

title: The external watchdog reports a memory stall but cannot freeze merges: the freeze hook requires writing governed state through the very runtime the watchdog must not depend on
rule_violated: PLAN Wave 2's early-watchdog item specifies 'anomalide breaker MERGE_FROZEN + operator notification'. The watchdog shipped with the notification half only: it files and updates an incident issue and fails its own run, but does not freeze merges. The omission is structural rather than an oversight - freezing writes the breaker ledger, which requires importing the ARIA kernel, and every failure the watchdog exists to catch is a failure of that kernel; a watchman that dies of the illness it watches for is not a watchman. The correct shape is therefore an alarm the MERGE side reads, not a write the watchdog performs: aria-merge-authority (already a required check) can refuse while a watchdog incident issue is open, which keeps the dependency pointing the safe way. Until that lands, a stalled ARIA memory is visible but not enforcing.
notes: Registered by the same session that shipped the watchdog (PR #1091), which deliberately carried the detect half only rather than wiring a freeze through a dependency that would silence it.

title: The project graph discovered projects from a hardcoded directory list the repository outgrew, so 38% of touched files - including 655 of ARIA's own kernel - were unplaceable and every plan touching them was refused as impact_graph_unknown
rule_violated: impact_graph._discover_projects enumerated six parent directories (apps, libs, platform/libs, web/modules, web/shared-ui, web/shell). That list was accurate when written; the repository then grew crates/ (6 nx projects), mcp/, tests/, tools/executors/, e2e/, scripts/, the Rust edge gateway, a standalone PWA under web/apps/, and ARIA's own Python kernel, and the list did not grow with it - a control that stayed correct only while its input stopped changing. A path the graph cannot place lands in unknown_files, which sets validation_scope to blocked_unknown_graph (impact_graph.py:46), which makes plan_impact return blocked_by ['impact_graph_unknown'] (impact.py:35). The failure is therefore a WITHHELD CAPABILITY rather than a wrong answer: measured on main at 36d5bf70 over the distinct files touched by the last 200 commits, 4282 of 11041 (38%) were unplaceable, of which 655 were aria-kernel/ and 449 sens-api-gateway/; plan_impact on aria-kernel/aria_kernel/ledger.py - the kernel's most depended-on module - returned blocked_by ['impact_graph_unknown','operator_scope_decision_required'] with empty direct and downstream project sets. Fixed by making discovery marker-driven (project.json as nx's SSoT, plus package.json/Cargo.toml/pyproject.toml for roots nx does not model), additive over the conventional layout so no existing project name or root can move, with the workspace root structurally excluded (this repo has a root Cargo.toml; a project rooted at the empty prefix matches every path) and shallow-first containment. Result: 50 -> 69 projects, unplaceable 38% -> 19%, the remainder being docs/, infra/, .github/ and .claude/ which are correctly not projects.
notes: Found while wiring PLAN Wave 3 Twin-lite into the cycle: the twin reads _project_graph, so the map ARIA was to consult about the repository inherited this blind spot wholesale. Known limit stated in the review doc rather than implied: the graph's granularity is the project, so an empty downstream_projects for a kernel file means no other PROJECT imports it - not that nothing depends on it. Within-project module edges are Deep Twin (PLAN Wave 10).

title: Twin-lite shipped CLI-only: nothing in the cycle refreshed the repository map and nothing in the cycle read it, so the map ARIA was built to consult was stale by construction and consumed by no one
rule_violated: PLAN Wave 3 delivers Twin-lite as the map ARIA reads instead of rescanning the repository - the operator's request was literal: work from a map, for token saving and for understanding. What shipped (PR #1104) was twin.py plus four CLI verbs (build/refresh/status/context). No CYCLE_PHASES row refreshed the map, so it was only ever as fresh as the last time a human ran a command, and a map consulted about a tree it no longer describes answers confidently about the past. No caller read twin_context_for_files either, so the compact per-file slice the module exists to produce reached nobody. Wiring only the refresh would have been strictly worse than leaving it alone: a phase paying git-log and parse cost every cycle to maintain a projection no consumer reads is this programme's signature defect inverted - not 'written but never called' but 'called and never read'. Fixed by landing producer and reader together: a twin_refresh discovery-stage phase (standard + burn_in, record_and_continue) keeps the map current incrementally, and create_agent_invocation_request attaches a repository_map slice for the files an evidence_ref points at, rendered in its own prompt section. The trust boundary is explicit and tested: the map is DERIVED data recomputable from the repo at indexed_sha, so it renders beside 'Impact graph refs' as orientation labelled 'not evidence', never inside 'Evidence refs (the ONLY admissible evidence)' and never in evidence_refs itself.
notes: Registered by the session that shipped Twin-lite in #1104 and then found, on trying to wire it, that PLAN Wave 3's three named consumers do not survive inspection: service examination would duplicate cached_service_analysis_order (already fingerprint-cached), and the regression-anchor gate would have its meaning changed ('did this diff leave a test' is not 'is this code covered'). Pressure churn/co-change remains the right Wave 5 consumer. The agent envelope is the consumer that matches the original request and needs no gate's semantics altered.

title: REQUEST_OPTIONAL_FIELDS is a contract vocabulary nothing reads: exactly one occurrence repo-wide, its own definition, and validate_request consults only the required tuple so an unknown field passes silently
rule_violated: agent_contract.REQUEST_OPTIONAL_FIELDS declares the optional half of the aria/agent-request/v1 vocabulary, but nothing reads it: a repo-wide search returns exactly ONE hit, its own definition at agent_contract.py:57. validate_request checks REQUEST_REQUIRED_FIELDS for absence and never consults the optional tuple, so an aria/agent-request/v1 envelope may carry any unknown or misspelled field and nothing refuses it. It is not a contract - it is a comment shaped like one. The root-cause fix is tier 3, make the wrong envelope detectable at validation time by rejecting fields outside required union optional, but it needs its own change rather than a one-line edit: the union must first be confirmed complete against every real aria/agent-request/v1 producer, and today the only producers in the repository are test fixtures (test_agent_contract.py, test_judge_envelope_migration.py, test_maintenance_agents_invariants.py), so completeness cannot yet be established from production usage. Same defect class as the project-graph blind spot (ORPHAN-HIGH-569): a declaration that never tracked, or stopped tracking, the thing it declares.
notes: Found while adding repository_map to the request envelope for the Twin-lite consumer. Adding the name to an unenforced tuple would be the appearance of a contract without one, so the new field got an explicit type check in validate_request instead - the same treatment impact_graph_refs already gets, which is itself evidence the tuple has been decorative for some time. CORRECTION applied 2026-08-06 before this entry reached main: the first version of this finding also claimed the tuple omits eleven-plus fields that create_agent_invocation_request really sets. That comparison was WRONG and is withdrawn. It conflated two distinct envelope types the agent_contract module docstring separates explicitly - aria/agent-request/v1, the strict Plan 016 contract envelope this tuple describes, and aria/agent-invocation-request/v1, the queue-layer row the minter emits, preserved unchanged for backward compatibility per operator instruction. Demonstrating that validate_request refuses a minted row proves only that the two schemas differ, which is by design. The surviving claim - the tuple is unread - was verified independently of that error and stands. The correction was made by removing the unpublished trailing entry and re-appending through add-explicit, because rechain-from correctly refused to rewrite chained history; the 1365-entry prefix was never touched and verified unchanged.

title: 21% of the ARIA kernel's declared controls have no production caller and nothing detects it: 18 of 85 control-verb functions were dormant, including the agent-envelope secret scanner
rule_violated: Four findings this programme closed are one defect wearing four names - a control that is correct, tested, exported and called by nobody: ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498 (a perimeter with no production caller), ORPHAN-HIGH-569 (a discovery list the repository outgrew), ORPHAN-MEDIUM-571 (a repository map nothing refreshed and nothing read), ORPHAN-MEDIUM-572 (a request vocabulary nothing consults). Every one was found by a human reading code; no gate has ever fired on this class, and a green suite is no evidence against it because the tests call the control directly - which is exactly how a control stays green while governing nothing. Measured: of 85 public module-level callables in aria_kernel whose names begin with a control verb (validate_, enforce_, assert_, require_, verify_, guard_, refuse_, check_), 18 were referenced by no production module at all - 21%. The most serious was verify_no_secret_in_envelope, whose own docstring calls it a hard-fail check that scans an agent response envelope before the kernel persists it, defending against agent stdout/stderr/validation_results embedding secrets: it was exported in __all__, covered by tests, absent from HARD_FAIL_CHECKS and called by nothing, while its sibling verify_no_secret_in_diff IS wired - so diffs were scanned and the envelope carrying agent output was not. Root cause is the absence of a reachability gate over the kernel's control surface; tests/invariants/invariant-reachability.spec.ts already proves the cure for TypeScript specs (declare, waive with owner/reason/expiry/finding, and compare the expiry to the CLOCK rather than to a regex) and that mechanism is now applied to the kernel rather than a second one invented. Fixed as tier 3: the whole class is detectable at test time from now on, the envelope secret scan is wired at the moment its docstring specifies, and the remaining 17 are declared dormant with owner, reason, deadline and finding rather than left silent.
notes: The gate caught a hole in itself during mutation checking, which is the strongest evidence it works: replacing the single call to verify_no_secret_in_envelope with pass, leaving the import in place, left the suite GREEN because an import counted as a reference. An import is not a use, and a control imported but never invoked is precisely the defect being hunted - so imports are now excluded via AST line spans and that mutation goes red. The 17 remaining waivers are not deferral: each names why the control has no caller today (a lane not yet live, a duplicate entry point pending a deliberate collapse, or a decision owned by PLAN Wave 6/8), carries a deadline, and fails the suite the day it expires.

title: format-scope.json carried three derived summary scalars with zero readers that made a cross-branch merge conflict structurally certain: five hand-resolutions in one day, none carrying information
rule_violated: buildFormatScope emitted file_count, managed_count and managed_file_list_sha256 alongside the ~9,300-element entries array they are computed from. Measured: one producer (buildFormatScope) and ZERO readers - getManagedFormatFiles, the manifest's only consumer, reads .entries alone, and a repo-wide search for the three names returns only their own assignment lines. Because all three change whenever ANY tracked file is added or removed, two branches conflict on exactly those lines regardless of which files each one touched, so a merge conflict here was structurally certain rather than occasional: five in one day once two sessions worked concurrently. Every one was resolved identically and none carried information, because checkManifest rebuilds the manifest from the tree and refuses anything that differs - so whichever side of the conflict is taken, the content is recomputed anyway. This is the derived-data-committed-beside-its-source defect: a checksum over a file's own contents, stored in that same file, cannot detect anything the contents do not already show. Fixed by removing the three fields (detection power unchanged - checkManifest still compares all entries byte-for-byte) and pinning their absence in BOTH the artifact and the generator, because a field absent from today's manifest but still emitted by buildFormatScope would reappear on the next regenerate.
notes: Found by counting rather than by irritation: after the fifth identical hand-resolution in one session the conflict was inspected instead of resolved again, and the mechanism turned out to be three lines that every branch necessarily touches. The neighbouring precedent is .gitattributes' merge=union for docs/reviews/orphan-findings.md, added by the parallel session for the same class of non-conflict; union is wrong here because the manifest is structured JSON rather than an append-only ledger, and removing the redundancy is better than teaching git to merge it. Deliberately NOT solved with a git merge driver: that would require registering merge.<name>.driver in every clone's git config, which does not travel with the repository and would change merge behaviour for everyone to work around data that should not exist.

title: A change touching both a placeable and an unplaceable path crashed plan_downstream_impact with TypeError, silently disabling impact-graph computation for the whole cycle
rule_violated: impact_graph.plan_downstream_impact sorted the set of resolved projects BEFORE filtering out the unplaceable ones: sorted({_project_for_path(p, ...) for p in ...}) followed by [x for x in changed if x]. _project_for_path returns str | None, so any changed_files list containing at least one placeable path AND at least one unplaceable path handed sorted() a set of mixed types, raising TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'NoneType'. Reproduced directly: ['docs/a.md','apps/farm-service/src/app.module.ts'] raises, while ['docs/a.md'] alone and ['apps/farm-service/src/app.module.ts'] alone both succeed - all-code produces no None and all-docs produces a one-element set that never needs a comparison, so BOTH halves of the obvious test matrix passed while the mixture crashed. The triggering shape is code plus its own review document, this repository's most common commit. Production reachability verified end to end: learning.py:222 calls plan_downstream_impact with a pressure event's evidence_refs, which are arbitrary mixes of docs and code paths; the local except GovernanceError at learning.py:228 does not catch TypeError, so it escapes the loop over every pending dispatch; learning.py:105's except Exception then swallows it into a generic learning_hook_failed governance event and the cycle continues. Net effect: one mixed-evidence pressure event silently disables impact-graph computation for an entire cycle, and the only record is a hook failure that does not name the cause. Fixed by resolving each path once into a (path, project) list, then deriving changed_projects and unknown_files from it - filtering before sorting, with the unplaceable paths still reported rather than discarded.
notes: Surfaced by an adversarial multi-agent investigation of the docs-only risk-class gap and then re-verified by hand before being believed - the same discipline that earlier the same day caught a HIGH drafted on a wrong comparison. A blind-spot sweep for the same pattern class (sorted over a comprehension of an unfiltered call) found 13 sites in aria_kernel; twelve are provably safe (as_posix, str, regex group, and a dict.get with a non-None default) and impact_graph.py:51 was the only real instance. TWO THINGS REMAIN OPEN and are deliberately not fixed here: (1) learning.py's narrow except GovernanceError means any other unexpected exception can still abort the whole dispatch loop and be recorded only as a generic hook failure - changing that alters another module's failure semantics and needs its own decision; (2) whether a docs-only change SHOULD be blocked as impact_graph_unknown is a separate question about impact._risk_class that this fix deliberately does not answer - it makes the measurement possible without deciding the policy.

title: A second path normalizer used lstrip as if it stripped a prefix, mangling every dotfile path into the impact-plans ledger: .github/x became github/x, which no project root can ever match
rule_violated: impact.py carried an inline second normalizer, item.replace(chr(92),'/').lstrip('./'), disagreeing with impact_graph._normalize_paths. str.lstrip strips CHARACTERS from a set, not a prefix, so any path beginning with a dot-directory was mangled: verified by execution, '.github/workflows/x.yml' -> 'github/workflows/x.yml' and '.claude/agents/orchestrator.md' -> 'claude/agents/orchestrator.md'. Two consequences, both verified: the mangled path is what plan_impact writes to the impact-plans ledger as the record of what a change touched, corrupting the audit trail; and no discovered project root begins with 'github/' or 'claude/', so the mangling also guaranteed such a path could never be placed by the graph, inflating unknown_files and pushing verdicts toward blocked_unknown_graph for reasons that were an artifact of the normalizer rather than of the repository. Fixed by deleting the second normalizer and calling the promoted impact_graph.normalize_paths, which uses removeprefix('./') correctly - tier 2, a second normalizer cannot drift from the first because there is no second normalizer. Blind-spot sweep: executor.py and codegen.py have their own _normalize_paths, but both delegate to _strip_relative_prefix which strips the './' prefix in a while-loop and was verified NOT to mangle dotfiles, so this was the only defective one.
notes: Surfaced by an adversarial multi-agent investigation and reproduced by hand before being believed. Sibling of ORPHAN-HIGH-575 in the same function family: 575 was the crash, this is the silent corruption, and both existed because path handling had two answers.

title: enforce_separation_of_duties runs on every agent submit and can never refuse: the field its decision depends on has no production writer, and the new reachability gate cannot see it because the control IS called
rule_violated: agent_contract.enforce_separation_of_duties reads sod = request.get('separation_of_duties') or {} then forbidden = sod.get('forbidden_agent_ids') or [] and refuses only when the submitter is in that list (agent_contract.py:367-369). It is invoked on EVERY agent submit (agent_invocations.py:2306). Verified by repo-wide search: 'forbidden_agent_ids' appears at exactly one production site - the enforcer's own read - plus three test files. No production minting path sets it. The control therefore always evaluates an empty list and its refusal branch is unreachable with production inputs: it is called, it costs a call, and it can never decide. The docstring's claimed property, 'implementer != reviewer for the same request_id' (Plan 016 Separation of duties), is not enforced anywhere. SECOND-ORDER FINDING, and the reason this is HIGH rather than MEDIUM: ORPHAN-HIGH-573's new control-reachability gate cannot detect this class at all. That gate classifies a control by name prefix and asks 'is it called' (control_reachability.py); this control passes because it IS called. The gate measures call-site existence, not decision efficacy, so the most dangerous member of the dormant-control class is invisible to the control that was built to police that class.
notes: NOT fixed in this change, and the blocker is a policy decision rather than effort - which is why no fix is guessed here. Making the control able to refuse requires deciding WHAT is forbidden, and the code expresses no such policy: deriving the forbidden set from prior claims for the same request_id (the ledger has request_id + agent_id and could supply it) would also refuse a legitimate retry by the same agent after a transient failure, and 'implementer != reviewer' is a role-separation rule the queue layer does not currently record roles for. Two honest options, both requiring the operator's intent: mint a real forbidden set at request creation, or delete the control because a check that cannot refuse is false assurance. A third option was considered and rejected as unshippable: make the enforcer raise when the forbidden set is empty, which would refuse every production submit today. A generalised 'vacuous control' gate was also prototyped and NOT shipped - a mechanical scan for controls reading dict keys no production module writes returned 10 of 68 live controls, but most were false positives from writers living in JSON/YAML or from two-character key names, and a noisy gate is one that gets waived into uselessness.

title: js-yaml CVE-2026-59870 blocks every merge in the repository: @nestjs/swagger pins the vulnerable 4.3.0 exactly, so bumping the direct dependency does not reach it

title: Twelve of the sixteen cycle learning hooks commit inside an unguarded loop: one bad item leaves the earlier writes on disk, skips every later item, and reports a wholesale failure
rule_violated: A cycle learning hook that processes a batch must contain failure per item. Measured: 12 of the 16 hooks in LEARNING_HOOK_ORDER, across 7 modules, commit inside a loop with no containment, so an exception on item k leaves items 1..k-1 committed to disk, skips items k+1..n entirely, and replaces the hook's whole report with one generic learning_hook_failed - a partial state indistinguishable from a total failure. ORPHAN-HIGH-575 was one instance of this shape (a TypeError escaping _impact_graph_compute's except GovernanceError, disabling impact-graph computation for an entire cycle); fixing that TypeError removed the instance, not the amplifier. A second defect in the same function: a refused computation was counted as skipped_no_evidence, so that counter conflated evidence-less pressures with graph refusals.
notes: Found by asking mechanically the question ORPHAN-HIGH-575 was only ever answered by hand. Fixed in the same change: aria_kernel/batch_containment.py provides guard_item (re-raising LedgerIntegrityError so a corrupt ledger still aborts the cycle, and returning (ok, value) so a legitimate None is never read as a failure); all 12 hooks are wired; _run_learning_hooks reports a hook that lost items as partial rather than ok and writes learning_hook_items_failed; telemetry emits aria_learning_hook_item_failures_total. The gate is tests/test_batch_containment_gate.py, which derives both the hook roster (from _run_learning_hooks's own dispatch tuple) and the definition of committing (functions transitively reaching a filesystem write) rather than hardcoding either - a hardcoded roster is the ORPHAN-HIGH-569 shape. Two false-positive classes were measured and fixed rather than tolerated: a name-keyed call graph merged same-named helpers so ledger.load_jsonl came out committing, and a record_ name-prefix seed plus bare .replace made _age_days a write primitive. The gate was also found blind: emptying its loop-body scan left the suite green because zero findings and zero vision look identical, so it now runs against synthetic known-bad input it must always flag. The waiver machinery is tested against synthetic waivers even though the repository declares none, and expiry is compared to the clock rather than merely parsed. Scope limit stated in the review doc: the gate covers the 16 cycle learning hooks only; the same shape elsewhere in the kernel is unmeasured.

title: The batch-containment gate covers 16 cycle learning hooks and cannot be widened as it stands: 'can reach a write' is too weak a proxy for 'commits this item', so a repo-wide scan floods to 91 candidates in 56 modules
rule_violated: ORPHAN-HIGH-578 shipped a gate that fails when a cycle learning hook commits inside an unguarded loop, and its review doc states the honest limit that the same shape elsewhere in the kernel is unmeasured. Measured now: reusing the gate's own machinery outside its 16 hooks returns 91 functions across 56 modules, and that number is NOT a defect count - it is the screen losing precision. The gate defines 'committing' as 'can transitively reach a filesystem write', which is precise enough inside the hooks (zero findings after wiring; read_jsonl, _finding_key, classify_pressure and _age_days all correctly excluded) because those hook bodies do not call the kernel's lazy root-initialisers inside their loops. Repo-wide it floods, because ensure_tools_dir writes repo_identity.json on first call and nearly every kernel function reaches it, so pure readers such as change_ledger.get_change_chain come out committing. A speculative narrowing was tried and rejected on measurement: dropping mkdir/makedirs from the write seed changed 92 to 91, because the leak is a real file write and not directory creation. Widening therefore needs a stronger notion than reachability - roughly 'writes a ledger row keyed by this item' - which is a design change, not a threshold tweak.
notes: Raised, not fixed, and deliberately not widened on a noisy signal - a gate that cries wolf gets waived into uselessness, which would cost more than the gap it closes. A real population does exist on live paths and was confirmed by reading rather than by the screen: memory.decay_stale_beliefs_by_age is a cycle phase (cycle.py:1064), pressure.close_pressures_from_signals runs from feedback.py:208/226, and memory._apply_diff_to_existing_beliefs commits per belief. Their true count is unknown until the definition is sharpened, so this finding claims a limit rather than a number. Incidental second defect found while sampling and recorded here rather than given its own ID: feedback_store.record_operator_feedback_batch has NO production caller - only tests/test_incremental_learning.py - which is the ORPHAN-CRITICAL-498 'called by nobody' class, and control_reachability cannot see it because that gate scans control verbs (validate_/enforce_/verify_/...) and this is a record_ verb. The reachability gate's verb-based definition is therefore its own blind spot, on the same evidence.

title: docs-check made docs/aria/CONTRACTS.md effectively read-only: 144 pre-existing markdownlint violations fire on the first person to edit the ARIA contract SSoT
rule_violated: scripts/ci/markdownlint-changed.mjs lints every changed docs/**/*.md and lints the WHOLE file rather than the diff. docs/aria/CONTRACTS.md has not been touched since ee92a9e9e (#934) and carries 144 markdownlint violations in main under the gate's own config, so it had never actually been linted. notes: 138 of 144 repaired rather than exempted: prose and blockquotes rewrapped (Prettier will not do this - its proseWrap is preserve, which is how the file drifted), bare fences given a language, list spacing and blank runs normalised, and the 578-character blockquote converted to reference-style links because its longest inline link was a single ~102-character unbreakable token. The rewrap asserts the token sequence is word-for-word identical before and after; that assertion earned its place, because a first attempt broke four long JSON string values across lines to satisfy MD013 and would have shipped invalid JSON in the documented examples - all four were reverted to their exact originals. The remaining 6 are string values inside fenced code blocks where MD013 cannot be satisfied without corrupting the example, which is the same reason tables is already disabled in that config; measured before changing a shared gate, code_blocks:false relaxes exactly 6 of 144 violations on main's copy, so it exempts code lines and nothing else.
